newsitem.title: HONG KONG: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - China bonds steady after Deng.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - China bonds steady after Deng.

text.p: China's dollar bonds remained steady in Asian markets Thursday after showing little immediate reaction to news of Deng Xiaoping's death, and analysts said that the outlook for Chinese credits remains positive.
"There really isn't any impact at all. If anything, the bonds are better bid because the uncertainty is out of the market," said a trader at a European bank in Singapore.
China's paramount leader Deng Xiaoping died late on Wednesday.
China's global bond due 2006 was bid at 74 basis point over comparable Treasuries and offered at 71 basis points in Asia, unchanged from its level in New York overnight.
The China global bond due 2006 has been trading in the 70-75 basis point range for many weeks.
Bankers said China credits traded in the international market had not been seriously affected by reports over the last several days that Deng was gravely ill.
The story has been the same for issues that trade more locally, traders said.

Syndicate managers said Bank of China's high-profile HK$4 billion floating rate certificate of deposit issue due 2001 was trading at 40 basis points over the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate, unmoved from recent weeks.
"There's no selling pressure. The news (on Deng) has been pretty much absorbed," said a trader in Hong Kong.
While most Asian bonds have had a stellar year, China bonds have performed particularly well due to improved sentiment toward China in the international investment community.

For example, the China bond due 2006 was launched last July to yield 110 basis points over Treasuries. China's century bond, which was launched at 299 basis points over the benchmark a year ago is trading around 135 basis points over Treasuries now.
Deng's death does not change the positive outlook for China credits, analysts said.
Any decline in China bond prices "would be a buying opportunity," a trader at a U.S. bank in Hong Kong said.
Traders said they would keep an eye on political developments in China in the wake of Deng's passing, but most said they did not anticipate a power struggle.

Both Moody's Investors Service and Standard and Poor's Corp said that sovereign ratings for China would be unaffected by Deng's death because that event should not change the direction of China's economic policy.
China is rated A3 by Moody's and BBB by Standard and Poor's Corp.
In other news, Moody's cut the ratings of three South Korean banks, citing the banks continued deterioration in asset quality and capital levels.
It cut the senior debt of Korea Exchange Bank and Cho Hung Bank to Baa1 from A3 and senior debt of Korea First Bank to Baa2 from Baa1.
Traders said the market had already factored in a downgrade for these banks and that their outstanding debt was little changed after the Moody's move.
Korean banks, especially those that have large exposure to troubled Hanbo, have seen their outstanding debt issues perform poorly in the secondary markets in recent weeks.
